name: Jaddua
title: Levite at the Reading of the Law in Rebuilt Jerusalem
summary: In the book of Nehemiah, Ajja is mentioned among the Levites who were tasked with explaining God’s law to the people during the great public reading at the Water Gate in Jerusalem. While Ezra read aloud from the Torah, Ajja and the other Levites conveyed its meaning in a way that was understandable to those gathered. This interpretive service was of crucial importance for the Jewish community after their return from Babylon, where many had lost familiarity with the sacred writings during the years of exile. Through the teaching of the Levites, the people’s spiritual grounding in God’s covenant was renewed, and the foundation was laid for a deeper, Scripture-based devotion in the restored community.

keyEvents.title: The Reading and Interpretation of the Law at the Water Gate
keyEvents.description: Jaddua was among the Levites who assisted when Ezra read God's law aloud to the assembled people at the Water Gate in Jerusalem. The Levites explained and interpreted the content of the law so that the listeners understood what was being read. This event marks a pivotal moment in the rebuilding of the spiritual life of the Jewish community after returning from the Babylonian exile.

versions.summary: Jaddua was one of the Levites mentioned in connection with Israel's return from the Babylonian exile. He is referred to in the book of Nehemiah as one who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it aloud. His role was linked to teaching and worship in rebuilt Jerusalem.
versions.title: Levite and Temple Servant After the Exile
versions.reason: [minor] The title says 'Levite and temple servant after the exile'. Although 'Levite' is correct, 'temple servant' is not directly attested in the text. Ajja's role is described more specifically as a teacher of the law/interpreter. A more precise title is suggested.; [major] Ajja is listed with the role 'priest', but he was a Levite, not a priest (kohen). Levites and priests were distinct roles in the Old Testament system. In addition, the role 'leader' for Ezra – his role was more specifically tied to teaching and interpretation of the law. The roles should be changed to 'Levite' and 'teacher of the law'.; [minor] Nehemiah 9:4-5 mentions a list of Levite names. It is uncertain whether Ajja (mentioned in chapter 8:7) is identical with one of the names in chapter 9:4-5. There is textual critical uncertainty regarding this, but it is reasonable to retain the reference with a caveat.; [minor] Neh 9:5-7 deals with the Levites' praise and God's greatness. Linking Ajja directly to this text is somewhat uncertain since his name is not explicitly mentioned here. The description should be moderated to reflect that this concerns the Levite group in general.; [minor] The summary is well formulated, but it should clarify that Ajja was a Levite (not a priest) and that his role was interpretation of the law rather than general 'worship service'.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a relatively obscure figure like Ajja, notes should be added concerning the meaning of the name, identification in the text, and the role of the Levites in the post-exilic period.

versions.summary: Jaddua was one of the Levites mentioned in connection with Israel's return from the Babylonian exile. He is referred to in the book of Nehemiah as one who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it aloud to the assembly at the Water Gate. His role was linked to interpreting the law and teaching in rebuilt Jerusalem, a task central to the Levites in the post-exilic period.

versions.summary: Ajja is one of the Levites mentioned in the book of Nehemiah in connection with the public reading of God's law at the Water Gate in Jerusalem. When Ezra read the law aloud to the assembled people, Ajja along with other Levites had the task of making its content understandable to the listeners. This interpretive service was of great importance in the restored Jewish community, where knowledge of the Torah had become weakened during the exile. The teaching of the Levites helped restore the people's spiritual awareness and anchor their identity in God's covenant and law.
versions.title: Levite and Law Interpreter in the Restored Jerusalem
versions.reason: [minor] The roles 'law interpreter' and 'law teacher' overlap significantly. It may be more precise to retain one of them and possibly add another role that captures the practical function, such as 'teaching Levite'. However, given our strictness with the third version: the roles are acceptable, though somewhat redundant.; [minor] The summary is well formulated and theologically correct. However, it closely resembles the two previous versions in its opening formulation. For the third version, the introduction should be varied more to avoid repetition.; [minor] The linguistic footnote conflates two different biblical names. The Hebrew עַיָּה ('Ajja'), meaning 'hawk/raptor', refers to a different person (e.g., Gen 36:24). The name in Neh 8:7 is likely חוֹדִיָּה or a similar variant. The name forms in Nehemiah 8:7 vary between manuscripts and translations, and the identification should be nuanced.

footnotes.text: The name of this Levite varies among different Hebrew manuscripts and textual traditions of Nehemiah 8:7. This makes the exact identification uncertain. The forms of the names in the list of Levites in this verse have been subject to textual-critical discussion.

The Levites' task of explaining the Law to the people during the reading in Nehemiah 8 is considered by many scholars as an early form of targum – oral translation and interpretation of the sacred scriptures from Hebrew into Aramaic. This practice later became a central element in synagogue worship.

After the Babylonian exile, the role of the Levites underwent significant development. From primarily serving at the temple with practical and liturgical duties, many Levites gained a prominent function as scribes and teachers of the people in the restored Jewish community under Persian rule.

The reading of the Law at the Water Gate (Neh 8) is regarded as a decisive turning point in Jewish religious history. This public reading and interpretation of the Torah for all the people strengthened the central place of Scripture in Jewish identity and laid the foundation for the later scripture-based character of synagogue worship.

The Water Gate in Jerusalem was probably located near the Gihon Spring on the east side of the City of David. Archaeological excavations in the area have uncovered structures from the Persian period that may be linked to the infrastructure and city walls of restored Jerusalem.
